claims.assertion: The driver deviated from the shortest/most direct route: the GPS track shows one off-route segment at 14:19–14:22 covering 2.15 km where the optimal route covers 1.38 km, adding 0.77 km and straying up to 1019 m from the optimal route (total trip 12.4 km vs 10.8 km optimal).

No exemption applies to that segment: the traffic record shows no incident anywhere near the route during the trip window (only moderate band-4 flow, 30–39 km/h, and fair weather), so the driver's 'my GPS rerouted me' excuse is unsupported by the only evidence RD-4 accepts.

The rider never agreed to the route change: there are no in-app messages at all between rider and driver, so there is no consent message timestamped before the 14:19 off-route segment start, and a post-hoc driver statement cannot substitute for prior agreement.

This is a non-metered RydeX fixed-fare trip ($25.04 all-in, surge 1.0×, no toll add-ons), so the deviation did not change the fare; under RD-2 the refundable amount is limited to the fixed fare's mileage component and here the billed distance (10.8 km) equals the optimal distance, so no mileage refund is computable.

The driver already has 2 upheld route-deviation disputes in the last 90 days, so this case makes the breach repeated and warrants an account-review referral to Ryde alongside the finding that RD-1 was violated.
Because RD-1 was breached but the computable refund under RD-2 is zero on this fixed-fare trip, the correct outcome is to dismiss the money claim while formally recording the driver's breach.

weaknesses: Our own case is weak on money: F4 shows the billed distance (10.8 km) does not exceed the optimal route (10.8 km) and F6 shows a fixed $25.04 RydeX quote with no surge (F5), so under RD-2 the computable refund is exactly $0 — the judge may well return no_action on the refund.

The rider's own complaint is factually off: they say 'the app estimated 11 km but ... the meter came to 11 km', and there is no meter on RydeX; the driver will lean on F6 (billed 10.8 km, fixed fare) and F8 ('nothing wrong with the fare') to argue the fare was correct, and the system records (F4, F6) back him on that point.

The deviation is modest — 0.77 km of extra distance in a single 3-minute segment (F3) within an overall +1.6 km / +15% trip (F1) — so the driver may argue it is trivial or GPS-optimised, and there is no minimum-km policy threshold (RD-1) to defeat that framing outright.

Traffic is not zero: band-4 flow (30–39 km/h) on AYE and CTE during the exact trip window (F9, F10) gives the driver some colour for 'traffic' even though RD-4 requires an actual incident (F11) and (b) alone cannot exempt a segment.

The rider's own profile (F13) shows 2 disputes in 90 days with 0 upheld, which the driver may use to paint this complaint as a pattern of unsuccessful claims, and our requested outcome rests on a violation with no monetary remedy.

events.title: Proposed ruling: no_action (model confidence 0.90)
events.body:
The trip was a non-metered RydeX fixed-quote ride: the total charged was $25.04 with a 1.0× multiplier, distance component $15.17 for 10.8 km, waiting $0.00 and platform $1.47, and the billed distance (10.8 km) equals the optimal route distance (10.8 km) [F4][F5][F6]. Under RD-2 the non-metered branch refunds only ERP/toll and unpublished add-ons incurred on an unexempted segment, and the fare breakdown shows no such item, so the computable refund is exactly $25.04 − $25.04 = $0.00 [F4][F6][RD-2]; the rider advocate's own withdrawal of the money claim (C4 conceded) matches this arithmetic [F4][F5][F6][FARE-1]. RD-2 expressly provides that a zero refundable amount yields no_action while still recording a violation of the shortest-route duty, which is the posture of this case [F4][RD-1][RD-2].

The deviation itself is established: the GPS record shows actual distance 12.4 km against 10.8 km optimal (+1.6 km, +15%), driven by one off-route segment 14:19–14:22 of 2.15 km where the optimal route covers 1.38 km, adding 0.77 km and straying up to 1019 m from the route [F1][F3]. RD-1 sets no percentage or absolute-km threshold, so 0.77 km of unexplained extra distance is a breach of the shortest-and-most-direct-route duty [F3][RD-1].

No exemption attaches to that segment. RD-4(a) requires a traffic incident on the replaced optimal stretch reported before the detour, and no incident was recorded near the route during the trip window; AYE and CTE showed only band 4 (30–39 km/h), which is neither band 1 nor band 2 and therefore cannot exempt a segment on its own under RD-4(b), and the weather was fair [F9][F10][F11][F12][RD-4]. RD-5 requires the rider's agreement to be timestamped before the segment start; there are no in-app messages at all between rider and driver, and the driver's statement that his GPS rerouted him is a party statement overridden by the GPS track and cannot supply prior consent [F7][F8][F3][RD-5]. RD-3 likewise finds no basis, since no rider-requested stop occurred before the segment [F3][RD-3]. The segment is therefore unexempted [F3][RD-1].

actions.detail: account action is never automatic; queued for Ryde review

what_would_change: Had an LTA incident been recorded on the stretch F3 replaced, before it started, RD-4 would exempt it (−$0.00).

claims.assertion: The driver deviated from the shortest/most direct route: the GPS track shows one off-route segment at 14:19–14:22 covering 2.15 km where the optimal route covers 1.38 km, adding 0.77 km and straying up to 1019 m from the optimal route (total trip 12.4 km vs 10.8 km optimal).

No exemption applies to that segment: the traffic record shows no incident anywhere near the route during the trip window (only moderate band-4 flow, 30–39 km/h, and fair weather), so the driver's 'my GPS rerouted me' excuse is unsupported by the only evidence RD-4 accepts.

The rider never agreed to the route change: there are no in-app messages at all between rider and driver, so there is no consent message timestamped before the 14:19 off-route segment start, and a post-hoc driver statement cannot substitute for prior agreement.

This is a non-metered RydeX fixed-fare trip ($25.04 all-in, surge 1.0×, no toll add-ons), so the deviation did not change the fare; under RD-2 the refundable amount is limited to the fixed fare's mileage component and here the billed distance (10.8 km) equals the optimal distance, so no mileage refund is computable.

The driver already has 2 upheld route-deviation disputes in the last 90 days, so this case makes the breach repeated and warrants an account-review referral to Ryde alongside the finding that RD-1 was violated.
Because RD-1 was breached but the computable refund under RD-2 is zero on this fixed-fare trip, the correct outcome is to dismiss the money claim while formally recording the driver's breach.

weaknesses: Our own case is weak on money: F4 shows the billed distance (10.8 km) does not exceed the optimal route (10.8 km) and F6 shows a fixed $25.04 RydeX quote with no surge (F5), so under RD-2 the computable refund is exactly $0 — the judge may well return no_action on the refund.

The rider's own complaint is factually off: they say 'the app estimated 11 km but ... the meter came to 11 km', and there is no meter on RydeX; the driver will lean on F6 (billed 10.8 km, fixed fare) and F8 ('nothing wrong with the fare') to argue the fare was correct, and the system records (F4, F6) back him on that point.

The deviation is modest — 0.77 km of extra distance in a single 3-minute segment (F3) within an overall +1.6 km / +15% trip (F1) — so the driver may argue it is trivial or GPS-optimised, and there is no minimum-km policy threshold (RD-1) to defeat that framing outright.

Traffic is not zero: band-4 flow (30–39 km/h) on AYE and CTE during the exact trip window (F9, F10) gives the driver some colour for 'traffic' even though RD-4 requires an actual incident (F11) and (b) alone cannot exempt a segment.

The rider's own profile (F13) shows 2 disputes in 90 days with 0 upheld, which the driver may use to paint this complaint as a pattern of unsuccessful claims, and our requested outcome rests on a violation with no monetary remedy.

claims.assertion: The rider's core claim of overcharging fails on the fare record: this was a fixed-quote RydeX trip, and the distance actually billed was 10.8 km, exactly equal to the optimal route distance with no excess billed, so no extra distance was charged.

Only one off-route segment exists (14:19–14:22, +0.77 km), and under RD-2 for a non-metered service the remedy is limited to ERP/toll and unpublished add-ons incurred on that segment; the fare breakdown shows waiting $0.00 and no unpublished item, so the refundable amount on that segment is $0.

The driver told the rider nothing in chat only because there was no chat at all (no in-app messages exist), and the driver's account is that the GPS re-routed him — but no refund turns on that explanation because the billed distance never exceeded the optimal route.

No traffic exemption under RD-4 is available: no traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window, and the only speed-band records are band 4 (30–39 km/h) on AYE and CTE, which is neither band 1 nor band 2, so RD-4(a)/(b) are not satisfied — this limits any discussion of 'reasonable cause' but does not change the $0 refund outcome.

The complaint is a single, first-time route dispute with no prior rider-side route violations upheld against this driver in the last 90 days on this matter: the rider has 2 disputes in 90 days, 0 upheld, while the driver's profile is mostly clean on fare conduct and the ride completed normally at 18.9 min versus 17 min estimated (+1.6 min).

weaknesses: The GPS record shows a genuine unexplained off-route segment: 2.15 km driven where the optimal route covers 1.38 km, adding 0.77 km and straying up to 1019 m from the optimal route (F3), with total actual distance 12.4 km vs 10.8 km optimal (F1) — the rider will argue this breaches RD-1's 'shortest and most direct route' duty.

There is no chat record of any route agreement before leaving the optimal route: no in-app messages at all (F7) and the driver only says 'I followed my GPS' (F8), so the rider will argue the driver never obtained the mutual agreement required by RD-5 before deviating.

The driver's profile shows 2 route disputes in the last 90 days, both upheld (F14), which the rider can use to argue 'repeated' deviation under RD-6 and to support a flag_account request, even though RD-6 requires this case to be upheld first.

The driver's explanation relies on GPS re-routing (F8), a statement rather than a system record, and it is contradicted by the fact that no traffic incident incident supports the reroute (F11) and speed bands were only band 4 (F9, F10), so the 'reasonable cause' argument under RD-4 will not hold.

points.response: Conceded on the money: F4 shows the billed distance (10.8 km) does not exceed the optimal route and F6 shows a fixed $25.04 RydeX quote, so no excess distance was charged and the refund is $0 — but D1 is silent on liability, whereas F1 (12.4 km actual vs 10.8 km optimal) and F3 (off-route segment 14:19–14:22, +0.77 km, up to 1019 m off route) establish the RD-1 breach independently of billing.

I accept the RD-2 arithmetic for a fixed-fare trip (F6 shows no toll and no unpublished add-on, so the segment refund is $0), but RD-2's zero-amount branch still requires the record to show the driver violated the RD-1 shortest-route duty, and F3 does exactly that — so the case cannot end as 'nothing happened'.

The absence of chat (F7) cuts against the driver, not for him: RD-5 requires the driver to obtain the rider's agreement before leaving the optimal route, and with zero messages no consent can pre-date the 14:19 segment start, while F8 is a party statement that the system GPS record in F3 overrides.
We agree there is no RD-4 exemption — F11 records no incident and F9/F10 show only band 4, not band 1 or 2 — which means the 0.77 km segment in F3 stands as an unexempted deviation under RD-1(c).

D5 misstates the profile record: F14 shows the driver already has 2 route disputes in 90 days, both upheld, so this ruling would make the deviation 'repeated' and supports a flag_account referral under RD-6, whereas the rider's own 0-upheld history in F13 is irrelevant to whether this driver breached RD-1 here.
Withdrawn as a remedy claim — I accept that on this non-metered trip the RD-2 refund is $0 (F4, F5, F6), so my client does not recover cash and I do not ask for one.

We do not contest that a single 0.77 km off-route segment occurred (F3) within an overall +1.6 km trip (F1), but RD-1's shortest-route duty is only breached where the deviation is unexcused under RD-3/RD-4/RD-5, and the money consequence is governed by RD-2, which on this fixed-fare trip yields nothing because the billed distance never exceeded the optimal route.

Conceded: RD-4 requires a traffic incident on the replaced optimal route, and F11 records no incident near the route while F9 and F10 show only band 4 (30–39 km/h) and F12 shows fair weather, so no exemption attaches to the segment (my own D4 says the same).

Conceded that F7 shows no in-app messages at all, so there is no consent timestamped before the 14:19 segment start and F8 (the driver's post-hoc statement) cannot supply prior agreement under RD-5; this point removes any defence of the segment itself but still leaves the refund at zero.

This is the decisive point and we adopt it: F4 shows the billed distance (10.8 km) does not exceed the optimal route, and F6 shows the $25.04 was a fixed RydeX quote with waiting $0.00 and no unpublished add-on, so under RD-2 for a non-metered service the only refundable items are ERP/toll and unpublished extras on the segment — both absent — making the computable refund exactly $0 and the correct action no_action.

We dispute the flag_account referral: RD-6 requires this case to be upheld first (RD-2 refund > 0 or an RD-1 breach recorded), and since no refund is computable and the fare records show no overcharge (F4, F6), the precondition is not met; F14's two upheld route disputes are profile facts that may never decide the case on their own.

We agree with the rider's own conclusion — the money claim must fail and the outcome is no_action — and we simply remove the gratuitous 'record a breach' framing: the ride completed normally in 18.9 min versus 17 min estimated (F2) and the rider was charged exactly the fixed quote (F6), so there is no basis for a penalty riding alongside a $0 refund.
